unmapped_findings: The 4Al (Fe-35Mn-4Al-0.1C) steel is described as an austenitic lightweight steel (single-phase FCC austenite), distinct from the 6Al (austenite-based duplex), 8Al and 10Al (ferrite-based duplex) steels [b0014, b0025].

Measured composition of the 4Al steel by wet-chemical analysis (Table 1, wt%): Mn 33.92, Al 4.13, C 0.094, Nb 0.11, V 0.11, Mo 1.20, W 0.98, Fe Bal. Only bulk 4Al composition is reported (no separate 4Al_γ/4Al_α rows in Table 1). [b0018]

The nominal composition in the Materials section is given as Fe-35Mn-xAl-1C-0.1Nb-0.1V-1Mo-1W (x = 4 wt%) [b0016], while the title/abstract use Fe-35Mn-xAl-0.1C; the measured C for 4Al is 0.094 wt% [b0018].

By SADP along the [100]γ zone axis, satellite diffraction spots near the γ reflections (related to Al and C concentration fluctuations / spinodal decomposition during quenching) are seen in all four steels and their intensity decreases with increasing Al content; for the 4Al austenite no {110} SRO/L1₂-type superlattice spot is circled in the SADP (Fig. 1e), unlike the 6Al-10Al steels [b0026, figure_001].
As tensile deformation proceeds for 4Al steel, the austenite microhardness increases with increasing strain [b0038, figure_003].

The 4Al steel exhibits typical three-stage strain hardening (stages A, D and E), in contrast to the 8Al steel's five-stage behavior, suggesting a different deformation mechanism [b0038, b0070, figure_003].
The stacking-fault energy of the 4Al austenite is 51.25 mJ·m^-2 at 23 °C (lowest of the four steels; increases to 62.64 for 6Al and 68.47 for 8Al) [table_002, b0029].
The density of the 4Al steel is 7.42 g cm^-3 (highest of the four steels: 7.42, 7.18, 6.99 and 6.84 g cm^-3 for 4Al, 6Al, 8Al, 10Al respectively) [b0016].
